title: Betting on a sequence
objectives: Value a bet on which of two patterns appears first.

screens.title: HH or TH?
screens.prose: Flip a fair coin until HH or TH appears. Each node records how much of a pattern you have built. Follow the arrows.

state.caption: Each arrow is one flip, with chance $\tfrac12$. The right-hand nodes end the game.

screens.question: What is the chance that TH appears first? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: What happens once the first T appears?
From T, the first H completes TH. HH would need two heads.
HH wins only if flips 1 and 2 are both heads: $\tfrac14$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac34$: TH wins unless the game opens HH.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows out of node T.

byKey.half: Both patterns have chance $\tfrac14$ in two flips, but this is a race. Once a T shows, TH must come first.

explain.text: HH can only win on flips 1 and 2. Any T before that means the next H completes TH first. So TH wins with $1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34$.

screens.title: HHT or THH?
screens.prose: Now the race is HHT against THH. The chain has more nodes, but the same idea works.

state.caption: Each arrow is one flip, with chance $\tfrac12$. The right-hand nodes end the game.

screens.question: What is the chance that THH appears first? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Once HH appears, what must happen next?
From HH, heads keep you at HH and the first T completes HHT.
So HHT wins only if flips 1 and 2 are HH. Any earlier T hands the race to THH.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when HHT can still win.

byKey.half: Same length is not the same chance. Any T before HH means THH completes first.

explain.text: Once HH appears, HHT is certain: the next T completes it. So HH must come on flips 1 and 2, or a T came first and THH wins. THH wins with $\tfrac34$.

screens.title: HHT or HTH?
screens.prose: HHT against HTH is harder: neither pattern wins at a stroke. Let $x_s$ be HHT's chance from node $s$.

state.caption: Each arrow is one flip, with chance $\tfrac12$. The right-hand nodes end the game.

screens.question: What is the chance that HHT appears first? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: From HH, HHT is certain: $x_{HH} = 1$.
$x_H = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 x_{HT}$ and $x_{HT} = \tfrac12 x_H$, since the start acts like H.
$x_H = \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 x_H$, so $x_H = \tfrac23$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac23$: fair odds are 2 to 1 on HHT.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write an equation for each node, then solve.

byKey.half: Same length is not the same chance. HTH can be cut off by the T that completes HHT.

explain.text: From HT, an H wins for HTH and a T sends you back to the start. Solving the node equations gives $\tfrac23$. So a fair bet on HTH pays 2 to 1.

screens.title: An even-money offer
screens.prose: A colleague offers you even money on HTH against HHT, first to appear. You would back HTH.
screens.question: Is the bet fair?

options.text: No: HHT comes first two times in three, so you lose on average
Yes: each pattern has chance $\tfrac18$ in any three flips
options.why: That is the chance at a fixed place. First to appear is a race, and HHT wins it 2 to 1.

options.text: No, it favours you: HTH overlaps itself, so it comes sooner
options.why: Self-overlap slows a pattern down: HTH waits 10 flips on average and HHT 8.

options.text: Yes: HTH waits longer, but the race is still even
options.why: The waits differ and so do the chances: HHT wins 2 times in 3.

hints.text: Equal chances at a fixed place are not equal chances to come first.
Use the chain from the last screen.
HHT first with $\tfrac23$.

feedback.correct: Not fair: you lose a third of your stake on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the race from the last screen.

byKey.b: You used the chance at a fixed place, $\tfrac18$ each. The race is different: HHT wins 2 times in 3.

explain.text: At even money your expected gain per £1 is $\tfrac13 - \tfrac23 = -\tfrac13$. Fair odds would pay you £2 per £1. Every pattern of the same length is not equally likely to come first.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Each node is the longest end of the flips that starts a pattern. **First-step analysis** on these joint states gives each chance. Conway's leading numbers give a shortcut. Let $A \cdot B = \sum 2^{k-1}$ over each $k$ where $A$'s last $k$ letters equal $B$'s first $k$. Then

$$\frac{P(B \text{ first})}{P(A \text{ first})} = \frac{A \cdot A - A \cdot B}{B \cdot B - B \cdot A}.$$
screens.question: What is $\text{HTH} \cdot \text{HTH}$?

hints.text: Compare HTH's last $k$ letters with its first $k$, for $k = 3, 2, 1$.
$k = 3$ matches (4) and $k = 2$ does not: TH is not HT.
$k = 1$: H equals H, adding 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $k = 3$, $2$ and $1$ in turn.

byKey.four: You counted only the full match. The last H also equals the first H, adding 1.
byKey.seven: You counted $k = 2$ too, but TH is not HT.

explain.text: Matches at $k = 3$ and $k = 1$ give $4 + 1 = 5$. With A = HHT and B = HTH the formula gives $(4 - 2) : (5 - 1)$. So HTH comes first with odds 1 to 2, a chance of $\tfrac13$.

screens.title: Solve it line by line
screens.prose: Interviewers want the equations, not only the answer. Solve HHT against HTH with one justified line per step.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Let $x_s$ be HHT's chance of coming first from node $s$.
From HH, a T completes HHT and an H keeps HH: $x_{HH} = 1$.
From HT, an H completes HTH and a T restarts: $x_{HT} = \tfrac12 x_{\varnothing}$.
From the start a T changes nothing, so $x_{\varnothing} = x_H$.
So $x_H = \tfrac23$, and HHT comes first with chance $\tfrac23$.
Each pattern has chance $\tfrac18$ in three flips, so $x = \tfrac12$.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `first_to_appear(a, b)`: the exact chance that `a` comes before `b` with a fair coin. A hidden helper `solve(rows, rhs)` solves linear equations in `Fraction`s. Then write `penney_sim(a, b, trials, seed)`, returning the share of games `a` wins.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.prelude:
from fractions import Fraction as _F

def solve(rows, rhs):
    """Solve rows . x = rhs exactly (Gaussian elimination)."""
    n = len(rows)
    m = [[_F(v) for v in r] + [_F(b)] for r, b in zip(rows, rhs)]
    for c in range(n):
        p = next(r for r in range(c, n) if m[r][c] != 0)
        m[c], m[p] = m[p], m[c]
        pv = m[c][c]
        m[c] = [v / pv for v in m[c]]
        for r in range(n):
            if r != c and m[r][c] != 0:
                f = m[r][c]
                m[r] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[r], m[c])]
    return [m[i][n] for i in range(n)]

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each; keep your own time and say each argument aloud. Give four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: TTH against HTT. Chance HTT comes first?
Fair odds against HTH beating HHT are $x$ to 1. What is $x$?
HHH against THH. Chance THH comes first?

hints.text: Ask when each pattern can still win.
TTH needs TT first; HHH needs three heads at the very start.
$\tfrac34$, then $\tfrac{2/3}{1/3}$, then $1 - \tfrac18$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first: TTH can only win if flips 1 and 2 are TT.
byKey.r1c1: Check the odds: HTH comes first with $\tfrac13$, so the odds against are $\tfrac23 : \tfrac13$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the last: any T before HHH means THH completes first.

explain.text: TTH needs TT at the start, else an H came first and HTT wins: $\tfrac34$. HTH comes first with $\tfrac13$, so the odds against it are 2 to 1. HHH wins only with three opening heads, so THH wins with $\tfrac78$.

screens.title: Follow-up: a biased coin
screens.prose: You gave $\tfrac34$ for TH against HH. The interviewer now uses a coin that lands heads with chance $\tfrac23$.
screens.question: What is the chance that TH comes first now? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Does the argument from the first screen still hold?
Once a T appears, TH still wins.
HH wins only with two opening heads: $(\tfrac23)^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find HH's chance first.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer. Heads are now more likely, so HH opens more often.
byKey.tails: You used the chance of a tail. TH also needs the opening to avoid HH.

explain.text: Once a T shows, TH still wins. HH needs two opening heads, chance $\tfrac49$. So TH wins with $\tfrac59$, even with a coin that favours heads.

screens.title: Choose second
screens.prose: An interviewer offers Penney's game for £10. They pick a pattern of three flips, then you pick yours. First to appear wins. They pick THT.
screens.question: Which pattern gives you the best chance?

options.why: HHT does beat THT, with $\tfrac58$, but TTH does better at $\tfrac23$.
Mirroring gives an even race, $\tfrac12$. You can do better.
TTT needs three tails in a row and wins only $\tfrac25$.

hints.text: Put a letter in front of their first two letters.
Their first two letters are TH; you want to finish just before THT can.
TTH: the opposite of their middle letter, then TH.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build your pattern from the front of theirs.

byKey.b: HHT wins $\tfrac58$ against THT. TTH wins $\tfrac23$.

explain.text: Take the opposite of their middle letter, then their first two letters: T, then TH. TTH beats THT with chance $\tfrac23$, worth £3.33 a game at £10 even money. Whatever three-flip pattern they choose, this rule wins at least $\tfrac23$.

ideas: Same length is not the same chance: TH beats HH 3 to 1, and HHT beats HTH 2 to 1.
First-step analysis on joint nodes gives every race exactly; Conway's leading numbers give it fast.
Choosing second wins: put the opposite of their middle letter in front of their first two.

formula.name: Conway's leading numbers
formula.tex: \frac{P(B \text{ first})}{P(A \text{ first})} = \frac{A \cdot A - A \cdot B}{B \cdot B - B \cdot A}
formula.note: $A \cdot B$ adds $2^{k-1}$ for each $k$ where A's end equals B's start.

summary.trap: Treating every pattern of the same length as equally likely to come first. That is true at a fixed place, not in a race.
